Get a glimpse of a GPU table's structure

Source: R/glimpse.R
glimpse.tbl_gpu.Rd

Prints a compact summary of a tbl_gpu's structure – row/column counts, grouping (if any), and each column's type with a preview of its first few values – similar to dplyr::glimpse().

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
glimpse(x, width = NULL, ...)

Arguments

x

A tbl_gpu object created by tbl_gpu().

width

Output width (defaults to getOption("width")).

...

Ignored (present for generic compatibility with dplyr::glimpse()).

Value

x, invisibly. Like dplyr::glimpse(), this is a side-effecting print method: it never transforms .data, so there is nothing to re-upload.

Details

glimpse() never collects the whole table to R. The preview values come from a small sample of the first rows, copied from the GPU as print.tbl_gpu() does, and the row and column counts and types come from the table's metadata.

A lazy table with pending operations runs its plan once for the preview (the result is freed when glimpse() returns; the table itself is unchanged), and one extra line starting Lazy: follows Columns:. If the plan fails (an error, out of GPU memory), glimpse() prints Rows: ??, the Lazy: line, the message and the stored schema instead of raising. A plan over a parquet file that does more than select or rename columns is not run for the preview.

Column value/type formatting does not attempt to reproduce dplyr's own glimpse() output (which is formatted via pillar) byte-for-byte – only the structural facts (row count, column count, grouping, column names, and column types) are guaranteed to match.

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  tbl_gpu(mtcars) |> glimpse()
}
#> Rows: 32
#> Columns: 11
#> $ mpg  <dbl> 21, 21, 22.8, 21.4, 18.7, 18.1, 14.3, 24.4, 22.8, 19.2, 17.8, 16.…
#> $ cyl  <dbl> 6, 6, 4, 6, 8, 6, 8, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 4, 4, 4, 4, 8,…
#> $ disp <dbl> 160, 160, 108, 258, 360, 225, 360, 146.7, 140.8, 167.6, 167.6, 27…
#> $ hp   <dbl> 110, 110, 93, 110, 175, 105, 245, 62, 95, 123, 123, 180, 180, 180…
#> $ drat <dbl> 3.9, 3.9, 3.85, 3.08, 3.15, 2.76, 3.21, 3.69, 3.92, 3.92, 3.92, 3…
#> $ wt   <dbl> 2.62, 2.875, 2.32, 3.215, 3.44, 3.46, 3.57, 3.19, 3.15, 3.44, 3.4…
